lead: The relative motion method finds the velocity and acceleration of one point of a rigid body when another point is known. Choose point A as the base. Point B moves with A, and also rotates about A. The velocity equation adds ω × r. The acceleration equation adds α × r and the inward term −ω²r. The method is used for slider-crank engines, four-bar linkages, pump mechanisms and door closers. Constraints such as a slider moving in a straight guide supply the missing directions, so two component equations solve two unknowns.
prereq: You need: 6.2 general plane motion, vector components, and the relative-motion ideas from Unit 5.

sections.h3: Velocity of one point relative to another

blocks.text: Points A and B are fixed on the same rigid body. The distance AB cannot change. So B can only move around A by rotation. Write the absolute velocity of B as the vector sum of the absolute velocity of A and the velocity of B relative to A. Some syllabi call this the relative velocity method.

blocks.where: v<sub>B</sub> is the velocity of point B in m/s; v<sub>A</sub> is the velocity of point A in m/s; ω is the angular velocity of the body in rad/s, positive anticlockwise; r<sub>B/A</sub> is the position vector from A to B in m.

blocks.text: The relative velocity v<sub>B/A</sub> = ω × r<sub>B/A</sub> has magnitude ωr. Its direction is perpendicular to AB. For plane motion, rotate AB by 90° in the direction of ω. If ω is anticlockwise, rotate AB anticlockwise.

A velocity polygon is the triangle or polygon formed by these vectors. Draw v<sub>A</sub> first. Add v<sub>B/A</sub> from its tip. The closing vector from the start to the final tip is v<sub>B</sub>. The polygon closes because v<sub>B</sub> = v<sub>A</sub> + v<sub>B/A</sub>. Use the known constraint directions: a slider point moves along its guide; a pin on a fixed link moves perpendicular to that link.

items: Choose a base point with known velocity, usually a crank pin.
Write r<sub>B/A</sub> from A to B using the given length and angle.
Write v<sub>B</sub> and v<sub>A</sub> with their known constraint directions.
Use ω = ωk and solve the x and y component equations.
Check that the relative velocity is perpendicular to AB.

sections.h3: Acceleration of one point relative to another

blocks.text: Differentiate the velocity equation. The angular velocity may change, so add α × r. The rotating vector ω × r also changes direction, which gives −ω²r.
a<sub>B</sub> = a<sub>A</sub> + α × r<sub>B/A</sub> − ω² r<sub>B/A</sub>
blocks.where: a<sub>B</sub> and a<sub>A</sub> are absolute accelerations in m/s²; α is angular acceleration in rad/s², positive anticlockwise; ω is angular velocity in rad/s; r<sub>B/A</sub> is the position vector from A to B in m.

blocks.text: The tangential term α × r has magnitude αr and is perpendicular to AB. The normal term −ω²r has magnitude ω²r and points from B toward A. This is the centripetal direction of B's path relative to A.

An acceleration polygon is drawn like the velocity polygon: a<sub>A</sub>, then α × r, then −ω²r, then close to a<sub>B</sub>. A slider's acceleration is along the guide, but a pin's acceleration has two components. Solve x and y components. Keep ω in rad/s; squaring a degree value is a common error.

items: Normal term: magnitude ω²r, always from B toward A.
Tangential term: magnitude αr, perpendicular to AB.
α is unknown in many linkage problems; one component equation gives it.

sections.h3: Slider-crank and four-bar at one position

blocks.text: A slider-crank has crank OA, connecting rod AB and slider B. A moves perpendicular to OA. B moves along the slider axis. Use v<sub>B</sub> = v<sub>A</sub> + ω<sub>AB</sub> × r<sub>B/A</sub> to find ω<sub>AB</sub> and v<sub>B</sub>. Then use the acceleration equation to find α<sub>AB</sub> and a<sub>B</sub>.

A four-bar has crank O<sub>2</sub>A, coupler AB and rocker O<sub>3</sub>B. Points A and B move perpendicular to their own fixed-link radii. The coupler's angular velocity comes from the velocity equation. Acceleration uses the normal accelerations of both cranks and the coupler.

Choose axes along AB and perpendicular to AB. The relative velocity ω × r has no component along AB, so the components of v<sub>A</sub> and v<sub>B</sub> along AB are equal. This shortcut removes one unknown before you solve. For acceleration, resolve along and perpendicular to AB; the normal term lies along AB.
Only one position is needed at a time. Repeat the same equations for the next crank angle. Plot v<sub>B</sub> or a<sub>B</sub> against crank angle to see the engine's speed variation.

figure.caption: The base point A has known velocity, B is constrained vertical, and the component solution gives the bar's angular velocity and B's velocity. Notice that the position vector is drawn from A to B.

spec.title: Relative motion method with the worked example
spec.aria: The relative-motion solution starts from base A with velocity 2.0 m/s right, uses the 1.2 m bar at 30°, solves the velocity equation with B moving vertically, and obtains angular velocity 3.33 rad/s and B velocity 3.46 m/s upward.

examples.question: Bar AB is 1.2 m long and makes 30° with the horizontal. End A moves horizontally to the right at 2.0 m/s. End B is constrained to move vertically. Find the angular velocity of the bar and the velocity of B.
steps: Take i to the right, j upward and k out of the page. Then r<sub>B/A</sub> = 1.2(cos 30° i + sin 30° j) = 1.039 i + 0.600 j m.
v<sub>A</sub> = 2.0 i m/s. B is constrained to a vertical guide, so v<sub>B</sub> = v<sub>B</sub> j, where v<sub>B</sub> is its signed upward speed in m/s.
Let ω = ωk. Then ω × r<sub>B/A</sub> = ωk × (1.039 i + 0.600 j) = −0.600ω i + 1.039ω j.
The velocity equation is v<sub>B</sub> j = 2.0 i − 0.600ω i + 1.039ω j. Match i: 0 = 2.0 − 0.600ω, so ω = 3.333 rad/s. The positive sign means anticlockwise.
Match j: v<sub>B</sub> = 1.039 × 3.333 = 3.464 m/s. The positive sign means upward.
examples.answer: ω = 3.33 rad/s anticlockwise and v_B = 3.46 m/s upward.
examples.check:
import math
vA = 2.0
L = 1.2
theta = math.radians(30.0)
omega = vA / (L * math.sin(theta))
vB = omega * L * math.cos(theta)
print(round(omega, 2))
print(round(vB, 2))

traps: Treating ωL as v_B instead of v_B/A. The relative velocity is perpendicular to AB, not along AB.
Dropping the −ω²r term in acceleration, or writing ωr instead of ω²r.
Giving the normal acceleration the wrong direction. −ω²r points from B toward A, not from A to B.
Using a velocity triangle when the directions are not perpendicular to AB and assuming a right angle that is not there.
Mixing degrees and radians, or mixing m/s with rad/s in the same equation.

quiz.q: Write the relative velocity equation for two points A and B on one rigid body, and define each symbol.
quiz.a: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A. v_B is B's velocity in m/s, v_A is A's velocity in m/s, ω is angular velocity in rad/s, and r_B/A is the position vector from A to B in m.

quiz.q: Why is the relative velocity v_B/A perpendicular to AB?
quiz.a: AB has fixed length, so B cannot move along AB relative to A. The only relative motion allowed by rotation is perpendicular to AB.

quiz.q: Bar AB is 0.8 m long at 45° above horizontal. A moves horizontally at 1.5 m/s and B moves vertically. Find ω and v_B.
quiz.a: r_B/A = 0.566 i + 0.566 j m. x: 0 = 1.5 − 0.566ω → ω = 2.65 rad/s anticlockwise. y: v_B = 0.566 × 2.65 = 1.50 m/s upward.

quiz.q: In the acceleration equation, which term points from B toward A, and why?
quiz.a: The term −ω²r_B/A points from B toward A because r_B/A points from A to B. It is the centripetal or normal acceleration of B relative to A.

quiz.q: What does the closing side of a velocity polygon represent?
quiz.a: It represents the absolute velocity of the final point, from the start of the first vector to the tip of the last vector.

quiz.q: A bar rotates at ω = 4 rad/s. AB = 0.5 m. Find the magnitude of the relative velocity of B with respect to A.
Why must v_A and v_B have equal components along AB?
quiz.a: The relative velocity ω × r_B/A is perpendicular to AB, so its component along AB is zero. The projection of v_B = v_A + v_B/A along AB therefore gives equal components.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multibody software such as ADAMS or Simscape builds these same equations for every link. Robotics uses the idea as the Jacobian relation between joint rates and end-effector velocity. Engine balancing adds inertia forces from acceleration analysis. Search next for 'relative acceleration method', 'four-bar velocity and acceleration', and 'Coriolis acceleration in rotating frames'.
